title: Wish: Regrets, Hopes and Desired Changes
summary: Choose wish or hope for a positive prospect, express regrets about present and past realities, and ask for a future change with wish + would or would not. Distinguish missing abilities and missed opportunities with could and could have.
learningObjectives: Distinguish hope + clause for a possible future from wish + noun in greetings and good wishes.
Express dissatisfaction with present facts and regret about finished events using appropriate forms after wish.
Contrast wish + could for a missing present ability with wish + could have for an unavailable past opportunity.
Use wish + would or would not for wanted changes and irritating repeated behaviour, not for fixed present facts.

explanation.heading: Wish someone well; hope that something happens
explanation.body: Wish can directly precede a person and a noun phrase when giving good wishes: wish someone success, a pleasant journey or good luck. Hope normally introduces a clause about an event that may happen: I hope you enjoy the concert. Do not put a bare noun phrase after hope in the same way, and do not use the regret pattern for an ordinary hopeful prediction.
explanation.example: We wish the new students every success, and we hope they settle in quickly.

explanation.heading: Wish + past for a present situation
explanation.body: To say that a current fact is different from what you want, use wish followed by a past form such as knew, had, did not or was/were. The past form marks unreality, not past time. Were is often preferred for hypothetical be, but was is also possible with singular subjects in everyday usage.
explanation.example: I wish the studio were closer to the bus station.

explanation.heading: Wish + past perfect for a finished past event
explanation.body: Use wish + had + past participle to regret something you did not do, or wish + had not + past participle to regret doing something. This expresses an unreal alternative to a completed past event. The past participle can be irregular, such as gone, seen, told or written.
explanation.example: I wish I had checked the opening hours before travelling across town.

explanation.heading: Could versus could have after wish
explanation.body: I wish I could describes an ability or possibility missing now. I wish I could have + past participle expresses disappointment about an opportunity that was unavailable in the past. The difference is temporal: can I do it now, or was I unable to do it then?
explanation.example: I wish I could have joined the hike last weekend, but I was working.

explanation.heading: Wish + would for a change you want to happen
explanation.body: Use wish + would + base verb when you want someone or something to act differently or when you want an event to occur. Wish + would not can complain about recurring irritating behaviour. The construction is especially useful when a change is outside your direct control; it is not the normal way to express a fixed state or your own present possession.
explanation.example: I wish the delivery company would give us a clearer arrival time.

explanation.heading: A current state is not the same as a desired change
explanation.body: Compare I wish the room were brighter (it is not bright enough now) with I wish someone would turn on another light (someone should take action). Use wish + past, not wish + would be, for fixed present states such as height, location or ownership. Wish + would can also convey impatience when someone keeps doing the same thing.
explanation.example: I wish the neighbours would not leave their bicycles across the entrance.

comparisons.title: Hope for an outcome versus wish someone well

left.label: Hope + clause
left.example: I hope you pass the driving test.
left.note: Passing is a possible future outcome.

right.label: Wish + person + noun
right.example: I wish you good luck with the test.
right.note: The speaker is offering good wishes, not describing an unreal situation.

comparisons.title: Regret about now versus regret about before

left.label: Present regret
left.example: I wish I had more free time.
left.note: Had is a past form referring to a present lack.

right.label: Past regret
right.example: I wish I had taken the earlier train.
right.note: Had taken is past perfect referring to a missed past choice.

comparisons.title: A fixed fact versus an action you want

left.label: Fixed situation
left.example: I wish the waiting area were larger.
left.note: Wish + past describes an unreal current state.

right.label: Wanted action
right.example: I wish someone would open another ticket window.
right.note: Would open asks for a change or response.

examples.sentence: I wish you a smooth first week at your new job.
examples.note: Wish + person + noun phrase is a conventional positive expression.

examples.sentence: I hope the outdoor performance goes ahead tomorrow.
examples.note: Hope + present-simple clause expresses an outcome that remains possible.

examples.sentence: I wish I spoke French well enough to follow the discussion.
examples.note: Spoke refers to a present ability the speaker lacks.

examples.sentence: I wish I had not left my umbrella on the train.
examples.note: Had not left expresses regret about a completed event.

examples.sentence: I wish I could have visited the exhibition before it closed.
examples.note: Could have visited refers to a past opportunity that is no longer available.

examples.sentence: I wish the people upstairs would stop moving furniture late at night.
examples.note: Would stop expresses a request for someone to change irritating behaviour.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I hope you good luck in your interview.
commonMistakes.correct: I wish you good luck in your interview.
commonMistakes.why: Use wish + person + noun phrase; hope needs a clause, such as I hope you do well.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I wish I know how to repair this camera.
commonMistakes.correct: I wish I knew how to repair this camera.
commonMistakes.why: Use a past form after wish for a present fact you would change.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I wish I would have taken more photographs yesterday.
commonMistakes.correct: I wish I had taken more photographs yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: Use wish + past perfect, not would have, for regret about an earlier event.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I wish I can come to the concert tonight.
commonMistakes.correct: I wish I could come to the concert tonight.
commonMistakes.why: Wish + could expresses a possibility that the speaker currently lacks.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I wish our apartment would be bigger.
commonMistakes.correct: I wish our apartment were bigger.
commonMistakes.why: Use wish + past for a current property of the apartment; would is for a desired change or action.

studyTips: First decide whether the outcome is still possible: choose hope for a plausible future, or wish + past for an unreal fact.
Make a timeline before choosing could, could have or had + past participle: now versus an earlier missed chance.
When a situation is annoying, identify whether you want a fixed fact to be different or someone to change behaviour; that decides wish + past versus wish + would.

exercises.prompt: A teammate is nervous about tomorrow’s interview. Choose a natural expression of good wishes: “I ___ you every success.”
exercises.feedback: Wish takes a person and a noun phrase: wish you every success.

exercises.prompt: The waiting area is too small, and its size is a fact now. “I wish it ___ larger.”
exercises.feedback: Were marks an unreal present state. Wish + would be is not normally used to describe the current size of a room.

exercises.prompt: You missed a concert last Saturday because you were ill. “I wish I ___ to it.”
exercises.feedback: Had gone is past perfect and expresses regret about a missed past event.

exercises.prompt: The supplier keeps ignoring your messages. You want a response. “I wish they ___ my emails.”
exercises.feedback: Would answer expresses a desired change in the supplier’s behaviour.

exercises.prompt: You do not know the route now. Complete “I wish I ___ the way.” Use the past form of know.
acceptedAnswers: knew
exercises.feedback: Wish + knew describes missing knowledge now.

exercises.prompt: The room is cold now. Complete “I wish it ___ warmer.” Use the hypothetical form of be; accept both common forms.
acceptedAnswers: were
was
exercises.feedback: Were is a common hypothetical form; was is also used for a singular subject.

exercises.prompt: You sent a personal message to the wrong group yesterday and regret it. Complete “I wish I ___ that message.” Use not + send in the past perfect.
acceptedAnswers: hadn't sent
had not sent
exercises.feedback: Had not sent changes a finished past action in imagination.

exercises.prompt: The bus is very late and you want it to arrive. Complete “I wish it ___ soon.” Use would + arrive.
acceptedAnswers: would arrive
exercises.feedback: Would arrive expresses a hoped-for change in the situation.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I wish I would have bought the train tickets earlier.
acceptedAnswers: I wish I had bought the train tickets earlier.
exercises.feedback: A past regret after wish requires had + past participle.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I wish I can understand the announcements in the station.
acceptedAnswers: I wish I could understand the announcements in the station.
exercises.feedback: Use wish + could for a missing present ability.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I wish the classroom would be closer to my house.
acceptedAnswers: I wish the classroom were closer to my house.
I wish the classroom was closer to my house.
exercises.feedback: For an undesirable present location use wish + past, not wish + would be.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Change only the first verb: I hope you a pleasant stay at the guesthouse.
acceptedAnswers: I wish you a pleasant stay at the guesthouse.
exercises.feedback: Change only hope to wish: wish + person + noun phrase is the normal greeting pattern.

speakingExercises.prompt: It may rain during tomorrow’s picnic, but you want dry weather. Say one sentence beginning “I hope”, using these words: the weather; stay dry; tomorrow.
acceptedAnswers: I hope the weather stays dry tomorrow.
speakingExercises.feedback: Hope + a present-simple clause expresses a possible future outcome.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your classroom is too small. Express the opposite as an unreal present wish in one sentence, beginning “I wish”. Use “our classroom” and “bigger”.
acceptedAnswers: I wish our classroom were bigger.
I wish our classroom was bigger.
speakingExercises.feedback: Wish + were or was expresses an unreal present fact.

speakingExercises.prompt: Yesterday you threw away your receipt and now regret it. Say one complete sentence beginning “I wish” using the past perfect of keep and the object “the receipt”.
acceptedAnswers: I wish I had kept the receipt.
I wish I'd kept the receipt.
speakingExercises.feedback: Had kept locates the wished-for alternative in the past.

speakingExercises.prompt: You cannot speak Japanese. Express this missing ability in one sentence beginning “I wish”, using could.
acceptedAnswers: I wish I could speak Japanese.
speakingExercises.feedback: Could after wish means you lack that ability now.

speakingExercises.prompt: You could not attend the workshop last month. Express regret about that missed opportunity. Begin “I wish” and use could have + attend + “the workshop”.
acceptedAnswers: I wish I could have attended the workshop.
speakingExercises.feedback: Could have attended refers to an unavailable past opportunity.

speakingExercises.prompt: You are waiting for a slow lift and want it to arrive soon. Begin “I wish the lift”, using would + arrive + soon.
acceptedAnswers: I wish the lift would arrive soon.
speakingExercises.feedback: Would arrive asks for a future change outside your control.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your friend repeatedly slams the door. Politely complain to your friend in one sentence beginning “I wish you”, using would not + slam + “the door”.
acceptedAnswers: I wish you wouldn't slam the door.
I wish you would not slam the door.
speakingExercises.feedback: Would not criticises repeated behaviour you want to stop.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences. You do not have a garden, but you plan to grow herbs on your windowsill next month. First make a wish to have a garden, beginning “I wish”. Then express your hope for the herbs using “I hope the herbs” and “grow well next month”.
acceptedAnswers: I wish I had a garden. I hope the herbs grow well next month.
speakingExercises.feedback: Wish + had describes an unreal present possession; hope expresses an outcome that may happen next month.

listeningExercises.audioText: I hope the open-air concert goes ahead on Friday. The weather forecast is still uncertain.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker want to happen?
listeningExercises.feedback: Hope describes a possible desired outcome: the open-air concert taking place.

listeningExercises.audioText: I wish I had kept my old bicycle. I sold it last spring, and now I need one.
listeningExercises.prompt: What earlier decision does the speaker regret?
listeningExercises.feedback: Had kept contrasts with the actual past decision to sell the bicycle.

listeningExercises.audioText: I wish I could have visited the gallery before it closed.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word verb phrase heard after “I” and before “the gallery”.
acceptedAnswers: could have visited
listeningExercises.feedback: Could have visited refers to a missed past opportunity.

listeningExercises.audioText: The flat is noisy now. I wish the bedrooms were farther from the street.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which present fact is the speaker unhappy about?
choices: The bedrooms are far from the street
The bedrooms are too close to street noise
listeningExercises.feedback: Wish + were farther shows the bedrooms are currently too close to the street.

listeningExercises.audioText: I wish my colleagues would stop talking during the presentation. It happens every week.
listeningExercises.prompt: What change does the speaker want from colleagues?
listeningExercises.feedback: Would stop describes a change in repeated behaviour.

listeningExercises.audioText: I wish I could speak Italian, but I hope I can enrol in a course next month.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which statement is supported by the audio?
choices: The speaker already speaks Italian fluently
The speaker lacks the ability now but may start learning
The speaker finished a course last month
listeningExercises.feedback: Wish + could expresses a missing present ability; hope identifies a possible future course.

listeningExercises.audioText: I wish the upstairs neighbours would stop moving furniture after midnight.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word verb phrase immediately after “neighbours”.
acceptedAnswers: would stop
listeningExercises.feedback: Would stop is the requested change in their behaviour.

listeningExercises.audioText: I wish I hadn't spent so much on the repairs.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the negative past-perfect verb phrase after “I” and before “so much”.
acceptedAnswers: hadn't spent
had not spent
listeningExercises.feedback: Had not spent expresses regret about money already spent.
